```{=html}
<p class="s1-takeaway">Neither prompt succeeds here. Even a correct “paris” would not reveal how it was learned.</p>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-source">Recorded original BERT-tiny MLM · expected answer: Paris · rank among the full vocabulary · inference without retrieval.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The objective rewards predicting text, not attaching a verified source to every output. Here the expected answer is known independently, and both top predictions are wrong. Do not claim that all pretrained models fail to recall capitals from this tiny checkpoint. Conversely, a stronger model's correct answer would not by itself distinguish memorizing a sentence, combining evidence from many documents, or applying a learned relation. Establishing training membership requires provenance evidence beyond a completion score. Prompt sensitivity is observable; the historical training pathway is not identified by these two runs.
:::

```{=html}
<table class="s5-table"><thead><tr><th>XNLI · zero-shot transfer</th><th>mT5-Large</th><th>ByT5-Large</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th>Clean accuracy</th><td>81.1%</td><td>79.7%</td></tr><tr><th>Character deletion: change</th><td>−18.3 pp</td><td>−11.4 pp</td></tr><tr><th>Character repetition: change</th><td>−12.3 pp</td><td>−5.9 pp</td></tr></tbody></table>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-takeaway">ByT5 loses less accuracy under these corruptions. Its clean accuracy is slightly lower.</p>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.13626#page=8">Xue et al., ByT5, Table 6 · unseen-noise column</a> · English fine-tuning, multilingual evaluation · pp = percentage points.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Both models have 1.23B parameters. ByT5 reads bytes; mT5 uses subwords. Noise affects premise and hypothesis. Deletion independently removes each Unicode codepoint with probability .1; repetition selects it with probability .2 and appends one to three repeats. These are accuracy changes from each model's own clean baseline, not error rates. The controlled noise protocol is broader evidence than one typo, but it does not isolate tokenization from other architectural differences or establish robustness under every real-world corruption.
:::

## Generalization and memorization can coexist {#learned-memory .s5-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="s5-two s5-memory"><div><b>GENERALIZATION</b><strong>Apply a learned regularity</strong><p>Training: “the dog is here”<br>Test: “the cat is here”</p><span>Illustrative new combination.<br>Verify that it was actually held out.</span></div><div><b>VERBATIM MEMORIZATION</b><strong>Reproduce a training passage</strong><p>Training: a distinctive passage<br>Output: the same passage</p><span>Check the output against<br>the training corpus.</span></div></div>
```
```{=html}
<div class="s5-evidence"><strong>604</strong><p>unique memorized training examples verified in a GPT-2 extraction study, from 1,800 selected candidates reviewed.</p></div>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-takeaway">Good average test performance does not rule out reproducing particular training examples.</p>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.07805#page=8">Carlini et al., Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models, §6.2</a> · selected candidates, not a random sample of ordinary queries.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The two boxes are conceptual examples, not records from the paper. In the published study, researchers generated 600,000 samples, selected candidates with extraction strategies, and verified training matches. The 604 verified cases establish that extraction occurred; their proportion among inspected candidates is not an estimate of memorization frequency for ordinary use. Correctness on novel examples and verbatim reproduction are compatible behaviors of one model. Recall of a common fact alone is not evidence of passage memorization.
:::

## Held out from which stage? {#learned-contamination .s5-slide}

```{=html}
<p class="s1-lead">A test question can be absent from fine-tuning and still appear in pretraining.</p>
```
```{=html}
<div class="s5-contamination"><div class="s5-corpus"><b>PRETRAINING CORPUS</b><span>Web documents</span><strong>Question Q + answer A</strong><span>Books and other text</span></div><div class="s5-route"><b>→ pretrain →</b><div class="s5-model">Learned weights</div><b>→ fine-tune →</b></div><div class="s5-test"><b>DOWNSTREAM SPLIT</b><span>Train: other questions</span><strong>Test: question Q</strong><span>High score may reflect exposure.</span></div></div>
```
```{=html}
<div class="s5-two"><div><b>Check overlap</b><p>Search for duplicates and related passages across all training stages.</p></div><div><b>Report provenance</b><p>Document sources, dates, split rules and the overlap checks you could perform.</p></div></div>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-takeaway">A clean fine-tuning split alone cannot establish that evaluation content is unseen.</p>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-source">Schematic contamination example, not a claim that our SST-2 items occurred in BERT-tiny pretraining.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Walk left to right. The test question is reserved when constructing the small labeled fine-tuning set, but it already influenced the weights in an earlier stage. This breaks the intended interpretation of “unseen.” It need not involve intentional cheating or an explicit answer column; passages that reveal the answer can also overlap. Deduplicating fine-tuning against evaluation is useful, but is narrower than auditing the pretraining corpus. Exact-match checks miss paraphrases and related documents. Document-level or source-level splits and genuinely later data can strengthen the design when their assumptions hold.

For our classroom experiment, exact normalized overlaps were removed between the sampled SST-2 training and validation texts. We do not have sufficient evidence to certify the validation examples absent from the model's complete historical pretraining. State that limit rather than treating the held-out accuracy as proof of exposure-free generalization. Avoid identifying a particular wrong or right response as memorization from its score alone.
:::

## Text prediction can inherit social associations {#learned-bias .s5-slide}

```{=html}
<p class="s1-lead">CrowS-Pairs: compare more- and less-stereotyping versions of a sentence.</p>
```
```{=html}
<div class="s5-noise"><span>paired sentences</span><b>→</b><span>score unchanged words</span><b>→</b><span>compare preferences</span></div>
```
```{=html}
<table class="s5-table"><thead><tr><th>Historical checkpoint</th><th>Preference for the stereotyping version</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th>BERT-base</th><td>60.5%</td></tr><tr><th>RoBERTa-large</th><td>64.1%</td></tr><tr><th>ALBERT-xxlarge-v2</th><td>67.0%</td></tr></tbody></table>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-takeaway">Predictive association is not factual truth or social endorsement.</p>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-source"><a href="https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.154.pdf#page=5">Nangia et al., 2020, Table 2</a> · 1,508 US-focused English pairs, nine bias categories · 50% is this metric’s symmetry reference, not a fairness certificate.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The paper masks unchanged tokens one at a time and sums their log probabilities, conditioning on the remaining text. It compares these pseudo-log-likelihood scores between paired sentences. The percentages count pairwise preferences; they are not classification accuracy or a calibrated probability of harm. The benchmark exposes particular learned associations, not every form of bias in every culture or application. Checkpoint sizes and training differ, so this table does not isolate the cause of the differences.
:::

## From a capability claim to a training question {#learned-scale-bridge .s5-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="s4-synthesis"><span><b>INTERVENE</b> change a controlled input</span><span><b>MEASURE</b> inspect outputs and failures</span><span><b>QUALIFY</b> state what the test establishes</span></div>
```
```{=html}
<div class="s5-bridge"><div class="s5-report"><b>OBSERVED BEHAVIOR</b><span>Context sensitivity</span><span>Agreement failures</span><span>Noise sensitivity</span><span>Recall and inherited bias</span></div><div class="s5-stream" aria-hidden="true"><span></span><span></span><span></span></div><div class="s5-decisions"><b>TRAINING CHOICES</b><strong>Which text?</strong><strong>How much repetition?</strong><strong>How large a model?</strong><strong>How many training tokens?</strong></div></div>
```
```{=html}
<p class="bridge-question">With a fixed compute budget, what should we change to improve what the model learns?</p>
```
```{=html}
<p class="s1-source">Next: modern pretraining at scale. The diagram poses design questions; it does not claim that more data or larger models automatically solve these failures.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Summarize the epistemic lesson: report the observation first and scope the inference to the experiment. Our small model responds to context but fails some simple tests; published studies show why robustness, training membership and social associations need separate evaluations. None is summarized adequately by one average accuracy.

The moving markers connect observed behavior to choices made before and during training. They signal the next investigation, not a measured causal improvement. Ask students to propose one change to the data or budget and one evaluation that could test it. Do not teach scaling rules or the next section here. Stop for instructor review before authoring Section 6.
:::
